danish.title: Fjerde bog (1806) — Kapitel 9
paragraphs: Den lille fyrstinde lå støttet af puder med en hvid hue på hovedet (veerne havde netop forladt hende). Tjavser af hendes sorte hår lå rundt om de rødmende, sveddækkende kinder, hendes charmerende rosenrøde mund med den dunede overlæbe var åben, og hun smilede glædeligt. Fyrst Andrej trådte ind og standsede ved fodenden af sofaen, hvor hun lå. Hendes glitrende øjne, fyldte af barnlig angst og ophidselse, hvilede på ham uden at skifte udtryk. »Jeg elsker jer alle og har ikke gjort nogen fortræd; hvorfor skal jeg lide så?« syntes hendes blik at sige. Hun så sin mand, men forstod ikke betydningen af hans tilsynekomst foran hende nu. Fyrst Andrej gik rundt om sofaen og kyssede hendes pande.
»Min elskede!« sagde han — et ord, han aldrig før havde brugt til hende. »Gud er barmhjertig ...«
Hun så spørgende og med barnlig bebrejdelse på ham.

»Jeg ventede hjælp fra dig, og jeg får ingen, ingen — heller ikke fra dig!« sagde hendes øjne. Hun var ikke overrasket over, at han var kommet; hun forstod ikke, at han var kommet. Hans ankomst havde intet at gøre med hendes lidelser eller deres lindring. Veerne begyndte igen, og Marja Bogdanovna rådede fyrst Andrej til at forlade værelset.
Lægen kom ind. Fyrst Andrej gik ud, og da han mødte fyrstinde Marja, slog han følge med hende. De begyndte at tale hviskende, men samtalen afbrødes hvert øjeblik. De ventede og lyttede.
»Gå ind, kære,« sagde fyrstinde Marja.

Fyrst Andrej gik atter ind til sin kone og satte sig i værelset ved siden af. En kvinde kom ud af soveværelset med forskrækket ansigt og blev forlegen, da hun så fyrst Andrej. Han dækkede ansigtet med hænderne og blev siddende således i flere minutter. Ynkelige, hjælpeløse, dyriske klager trængte gennem døren. Fyrst Andrej rejste sig, gik hen til døren og forsøgte at åbne den. Nogen holdt den lukket.
»De kan ikke komme ind! De kan ikke!« sagde en forskrækket stemme indefra.

Han begyndte at vandre frem og tilbage. Skriget holdt op, og der gik endnu et par sekunder. Så lød pludselig et forfærdeligt skrig — det kunne ikke være hendes, hun kunne ikke skrige sådan — fra soveværelset. Fyrst Andrej løb til døren; skriget ophørte, og han hørte et spædbarnsskrig.
»Hvorfor har de taget en baby derind?« tænkte fyrst Andrej i det første sekund. »En baby? Hvilken baby ...? Hvorfor er der en baby der? Eller er barnet født?«

Så indså han pludselig den glædelige betydning af det skrig; tårerne kvalte ham, og idet han støttede albuerne på vindueskarmen, begyndte han at græde og hulke som et barn. Døren gik op. Lægen med oprullede skjorteærmer, uden frakke, bleg og med en dirrende kæbe, kom ud af værelset. Fyrst Andrej vendte sig mod ham, men lægen sendte ham et forvildet blik og gik forbi uden et ord. En kvinde styrtede ud, og da hun så fyrst Andrej, standsede hun tøvende på tærsklen. Han gik ind til sin kone. Hun lå død i den samme stilling, han havde set hende i fem minutter forinden, og trods de stive øjne og kindens bleghed, lå det samme udtryk i hendes charmerende, barnlige ansigt med den dunede overlæbe.
»Jeg elsker jer alle, og jeg har ikke gjort nogen fortræd; og hvad har I gjort ved mig?« — sagde hendes charmerende, ynkelige, døde ansigt.
I et hjørne af rummet grynte og peb noget rødt og bitte lille i Marja Bogdanovnas dirrende, hvide hænder.

To timer senere gik fyrst Andrej stille ind i sin fars værelse. Den gamle mand vidste allerede alt. Han stod tæt ved døren, og så snart den åbnedes, sluttede hans ru, gamle arme sig som en skruestik om sin søns hals, og uden et ord begyndte han at hulke som et barn.

Tre dage senere blev den lille fyrstinde begravet, og fyrst Andrej gik op ad trinnene til det sted, hvor kisten stod, for at give hende det sidste kys. Og der i kisten lå det samme ansigt, skønt med lukkede øjne. »Ak, hvad har I gjort ved mig?« syntes det stadig at sige, og fyrst Andrej følte, at noget brast i hans sjæl, og at han var skyldig i en synd, han hverken kunne sone eller glemme. Han kunne ikke græde. Den gamle mand kom også hen og kyssede de voksagtige små hænder, der lå stille krydset over brystet, og også for ham syntes ansigtet at sige: »Ak, hvad har I gjort ved mig, og hvorfor?« Og ved det syn vendte den gamle mand sig vredt bort.
Endnu fem dage gik, og den lille fyrst Nikolaj Andrejevitj blev døbt. Ammen holdt dåbstæppet med hagen, mens præsten med en gåsefjer salvede den lille drengs rødmende, rynkede fodsåler og håndflader.

Hans bedstefar, der var gudfar, skælvede og var bange for at tabe ham, mens han bar barnet rundt om den buklede tindøbefont og overdrog det til gudmoderen, fyrstinde Marja. Fyrst Andrej sad i et andet værelse, svimmel af angst for at barnet skulle drukne i fonten, og ventede på ceremoniens afslutning. Han så glad op på barnet, da ammen bragte det til ham, og nikkede godkendende, da hun fortalte ham, at vokset med barnets hår ikke var sunket i fonten, men havde flydt oven på.

english.title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: The little princess lay propped up on pillows, a white cap on her head — the contractions had just stopped for the moment. Strands of her black hair clung to her flushed, perspiring cheeks. Her lovely rosy mouth with its downy lip was open and she was smiling happily. Prince Andrew came in and stopped at the foot of the sofa where she lay. Her shining eyes, filled with childlike fear and excitement, rested on him without changing expression. "I love everyone and have never harmed anyone — so why must I suffer like this? Help me!" her look seemed to say. She saw her husband but didn't grasp what his appearance here and now really meant. Prince Andrew walked around the sofa and kissed her forehead.
"My darling!" he said — a word he had never used with her before. "God is merciful...."
She looked at him with an inquiring, childlike reproach.

"I was counting on you for help, and I get none — none from you either!" her eyes seemed to say. She wasn't surprised that he had come; she didn't fully register his arrival. His being there had nothing to do with her suffering or with easing it. The contractions started again and Mary Bogdanovna advised Prince Andrew to leave the room.
The doctor arrived. Prince Andrew went out and, meeting Princess Mary, joined her again. They began talking in whispers, but their conversation kept breaking off. They waited and listened.
"Go to her, dear," said Princess Mary.

Prince Andrew went back to his wife and sat waiting in the room next to hers. A woman came out of the bedroom with a frightened face and became flustered when she saw Prince Andrew. He covered his face with his hands and stayed like that for several minutes. Pitiful, helpless, animal moans came through the door. Prince Andrew stood up, went to the door, and tried to open it. Someone was holding it shut from inside.
"You can't come in! You can't!" said a terrified voice from within.

He began pacing the room. The screaming stopped, and a few more seconds passed. Then suddenly a terrible shriek — it couldn't be hers, she couldn't scream like that — came from the bedroom. Prince Andrew ran to the door; the scream cut off and he heard the wail of a newborn.
"Why have they brought a baby in there?" thought Prince Andrew in the first instant. "A baby? What baby...? Why is there a baby? Or has the baby been born?"

Then suddenly he grasped the joyful meaning of that cry. Tears choked him, and leaning his elbows on the windowsill, he began to weep, sobbing like a child. The door opened. The doctor emerged with his sleeves rolled up, without his coat, pale and with a trembling jaw. Prince Andrew turned to him, but the doctor gave him a dazed look and walked past without a word. A woman rushed out and, seeing Prince Andrew, hesitated on the threshold. He went into his wife's room. She was lying dead, in the same position he had seen her in five minutes before. Despite the fixed stare and the pallor of her cheeks, the same expression remained on her lovely, childlike face with its upper lip covered in fine dark hair.
"I love everyone, and I've never harmed anyone — and what have you done to me?" said her beautiful, pitiful, lifeless face.
In a corner of the room something red and tiny grunted and squealed in Mary Bogdanovna's trembling white hands.

Two hours later Prince Andrew, stepping softly, went into his father's room. The old man already knew everything. He was standing near the door, and as soon as it opened, his rough old arms closed like a vise around his son's neck. Without a word, he began to sob like a child.

Three days later the little princess was buried, and Prince Andrew went up the steps to where the coffin stood to give her a final kiss. There in the coffin lay the same face, though now with closed eyes. "Ah, what have you done to me?" it still seemed to say. And Prince Andrew felt something give way in his soul — he was guilty of a sin he could neither undo nor forget. He couldn't weep. The old man came up too and kissed the small waxen hands lying quietly crossed on her chest, and to him as well her face seemed to say: "Ah, what have you done to me, and why?" And at the sight, the old man turned angrily away.

Another five days passed, and then the young Prince Nikolai Andreevich was baptized. The wet nurse held the coverlet with her chin while the priest used a goose feather to anoint the baby's small red, wrinkled soles and palms.

His grandfather, who was his godfather, trembling and afraid of dropping him, carried the infant around the battered tin font and handed him over to the godmother, Princess Mary. Prince Andrew sat in another room, faint with fear that the baby might be dropped into the font, and waited for the ceremony to end. He looked up joyfully at the baby when the nurse brought him over, and nodded his approval when she told him that the wax with the baby's hair had not sunk in the font but had floated.
